transcript:
HEADER: 2026-03-28 15:00 PDT | Duration ~62m | Attendees: Maya, Alex, Priya (Redwood) -- Samir, Elena, Jordan, Toby (ZenithTech)

Summary: Quick deep-dive to compare runtime profiles between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM routes for Zenith's 2.7B model; focus on kernel selection, cuda graphs reuse, kv cache behavior, and quantization impact.

00:00:05 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round of intros, we have Alex our lead SE who did the profiling, Priya on infra, and from Zenith?
00:00:15 Samir: hey Samir here, ML infra lead, elena and jordan are with me. thanks for doing this.
00:00:25 Alex: cool, i'll kick off with a quick overview of the test harness we used, then we'll show traces. note, transcript might have small mis-hearings on acronyms.

00:01:10 Alex: ok, test setup: A100 80GB, Ubuntu 22.04, cuda 12.1, cudnn matching, TRT-LLM 1.2. We ran both TensorRT-LLM (trt-llm path) and vLLM (optimized pytorch path) with the same model weights, single-model sharded on one GPU to keep apples-to-apples.
00:01:45 Elena: question — were you using CUDA graphs for both paths or just TRT?
00:01:50 Alex: good question. we used cuda graphs for both where feasible; trt-llm has tighter integration so the graphs get replayed more effectively on repeated seq lengths. vLLM used graph capture around the attention kernel and matmuls, but it was more manual.

00:03:10 Alex: first slide: p50 latency at batch=1 with seq=128, trt-llm p50 ~78ms, vllm p50 ~95ms. throughput (tokens/sec) trt-llm ~1,250, vllm ~980 on this workload. p95 tells a different story: trt-llm p95 ~310ms, vllm p95 ~270ms — that's because vLLM's dynamic batching sometimes evens out tails with its request coalescer.
00:03:50 Jordan: that p95 difference surprised me. is that due to kernel selection or queuing?
00:03:55 Alex: a combo. trt-llm uses highly optimized fused kernels that are faster per-op but have harder worst-case scheduling when batch sizes vary; vLLM's scheduler batches requests and amortizes overheads. Also we saw kernel-launch latency dominating some small-batch cases.

00:05:30 Alex: kernel selection detail: we have multiple GEMM/attention kernels — some are fp16-tuned, some use tensor cores with different tiling. TRT path prefers large tiled kernels which give best steady-state throughput; vLLM route sometimes picks smaller kernels to reduce workspace or latency. We instrumented kernel timelines (nvprof/nvtx) — see trace link we shared in chat.
00:06:05 Samir: do you have guidance on forcing kernel choices? we hit an issue where a particular attention kernel regresses perf on longer seqs.
00:06:12 Priya: we can pin kernels via our runtime flags; Alex can show the config. we also have an autotuner that picks best kernel per layer after warmup.
00:06:25 Alex: yes, the autotuner runs short microbenchmarks per layer and will pick kernel variants per sequence bucket. it helps a lot when you have mixed seq lengths. downside: warmup cost and slight complexity in determinism.

00:08:00 Alex: CUDA graphs — both paths benefit, but TRT gets a larger win because more of the compute graph is fused. For repeated same-seqlen inference, we saw up to 20% lower p50 and 25% higher throughput once graphs are warmed. With variable seqlen, graph reuse drops. you can keep some graph buckets for top N seq lengths to cover most requests.
00:08:35 Elena: how big is the graph memory footprint? we worry about memory if we keep many buckets.
00:08:40 Alex: good point — each graph has overhead (captures and associated temp memory). on A100 we recommend keeping 3-5 common buckets; beyond that the marginal benefit falls and memory pressure rises. we documented heuristics in the shared doc.

00:10:10 Alex: next, KV cache: we observed that trt-llm uses a contiguous KV layout that's very GPU friendly. vLLM stores KV in host-managed buffers with a bounce/transfer in some pathways depending on config. For large-context workloads (seq 2k+), trt-llm's KV layout was ~15% lower latency because it avoids extra H2D copies, but it does require more VRAM reservation.
00:10:45 Elena: we do long-context for retrieval-augmented uses, 4k sometimes. will that fit?
00:10:50 Alex: for 4k, with 2.7B, you'd be toward the upper end of A100 VRAM. We recommended either dedicated capacity with reserved VRAM or using quantization.

00:12:20 Alex: quantization: we benchmarked q8_0, q4_0, and dynamic mixed-precision. q8 preserved latency and throughput well, q4 had larger accuracy delta on certain tokens but gave ~1.8x tokens/sec improvement. note: on TRT path some quant kernels are in beta and kernel selection differs. vLLM's quant path is more conservative but stable.
00:13:05 Samir: accuracy matters for us; we need to preserve top-k token distributions for scoring use-cases. can you run evals on our eval set?
00:13:10 Alex: yes, that's part of the action items — we'll run token-level regression checks on your prompt set after we receive it.

00:14:40 Alex: batching strategy: three levers — request batch size, internal microbatching, and prefix caching. For low-latency interactive apps we recommend small batch sizes and aggressive prefix KV caching for repeated prompts. For throughput-first (e.g., offline generation) go larger batch sizes and fuse more ops.
00:15:10 Jordan: what's the impact on tail latency if we increase batch size to 8?
00:15:15 Alex: for batch=8 on seq=256 we saw trt-llm tokens/sec jump to ~3,900 and p95 ~420ms. vLLM throughput improved similarly but its p95 stayed a bit lower because of dynamic coalescing. tail latency grows with batch size because of wait for batch fill — we can mitigate with adaptive batching (timeout thresholds).

00:17:00 Alex: about eviction and KV cache behavior under memory pressure — trt-llm will evict whole prefix buckets; vLLM tends to evict more granularly. eviction policy affects quality for RAG because if the prefix is evicted you pay for recomputing key/value states. we saw that for mixed workloads eviction can spike p99.
00:17:30 Toby: our SRE asks if Redwood supports persistent KV cache across container restarts in private deployments?
00:17:35 Priya: not persistently today; we snapshot cache warmup patterns and can pre-warm on restart. persistent on-disk KV cache is on the roadmap for private installs. for Dedicated we can do checkpoint restores to speed warmup.

00:19:40 Alex: network/VPC considerations: if you go private VPC with model file pull from S3 in a controlled subnet, ensure NVMe scratch is in same subnet for prefetch speed. Also KMS key access should be low-latency; we recommend colocating KMS regional endpoints.
00:20:10 Jordan: security checklist?
00:20:12 Maya: we'll share our SOC2 summary and SAML/SCIM integration notes — action item for Maya to send.

00:21:30 Alex: demo of trace: showing nvtx timeline. you can see fused attention kernel at 00:21:45, then a block of small GEMMs. in TRT path the fused block is single large kernel; in vLLM it's multiple smaller ops. this maps to the latency/throughput behavior.
00:22:40 Elena: any easy knobs to change kernel selection without rebuilding?
00:22:45 Alex: runtime flags: prefer_fused_attention=true, and another flag to prefer workspace-heavy kernels. also environment variable to disable particular kernel IDs if you see regressions. we can give you a script to toggle and repro.

00:24:50 Alex: measurement caveats: make sure to run long enough to capture steady state and include cold-start warmup — graphs need 10-50 iterations depending on complexity. also isolate GPU from other noisy tenants; run with NVML to track GPU clock/power.

00:26:10 Samir: what about multi-model packing on one GPU? we sometimes host 3 smaller models per card. how does TRT handle that?
00:26:20 Alex: packing works but reduces ability to use huge fused kernels since memory layout constraints require smaller workspace. vLLM packing tends to be more flexible. the trade is throughput per model vs overall utilization. we can run a packing test for your footprint.

00:28:00 Alex: quick note on determinism: tensor core variations and kernel selection can change floating outputs slightly; if you need exact bitwise repeatability we have modes that trade perf for determinism.

00:30:15 Alex: benchmark plan proposal: Redwood runs 3 scenarios — interactive (batch1 seq128), mid-ctx (batch2 seq512), long-ctx (batch1 seq2048 with kv). compare trt-llm, vllm, and trt-llm+q4 and report p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and memory usage.
00:30:40 Samir: that sounds perfect. we will provide prompts and a model checkpoint sanitized.

00:31:50 Priya: about deployment: for on-prem we give an install bundle with a control plane that respects your network policies; for fully air-gapped we'll need explicit planning for KMS and telemetry.
00:32:10 Jordan: air-gapped is required for a subset of our customers — can we get an estimated timeline for private install?
00:32:20 Maya: standard private deployments take 6-8 weeks for initial install + connectivity review; air-gapped adds 2-3 weeks for packaging approvals. we'll follow up with checklist.

00:34:05 Alex: back to traces — showed CUDA graph warmup effect: iteration 1-10 high variance, after ~15 iterations graphs replay and variance collapses. with mixed seq lengths variance returns.
00:34:45 Elena: is there an easy way to pre-warm graphs with representative traffic?
00:34:50 Alex: yes — a synthetic pre-warm job that replays your prompt set at low concurrency; we can orchestrate that as part of deployment.

00:36:30 Alex: troubleshooting notes: when you see a regression, capture nvtx, kernel names, and the workspace sizes. also check for asynchronous memcpy stalls — sometimes host-to-device queues get blocked.

00:38:10 Samir: curious about cost tradeoffs — if we pick trt and dedicate A100s vs vLLM on shared pods what's rough cost delta?
00:38:20 Maya: rough ballpark — TRT path with Dedicated will likely need fewer GPUs for same tokens/sec (20-35% fewer), so infra cost lower but engineering/integration might be higher and need reserved capacity. vLLM on shared can be more flexible with bursty loads. we'll put numbers in the perf report.

00:40:00 Alex: we also noticed tiny regressions with a particular attention pattern (long key, short query) — that's a kernel tiling mismatch; the autotuner fixed it in our test after one warmup run.

00:42:00 Jordan: regarding encryption-in-use with KMS and HSM, any perf penalty?
00:42:10 Priya: KMS calls are only at model load or key roll; runtime crypto for tensors is GPU-native where supported, negligible perf impact for inference. network egress to KMS must be low-latency though.

00:43:30 Alex: follow-up: we'll attach raw cuda graphs and a condensed kernel timeline in the run report. also provide recommended kernel flags per-layer as a starting point.

00:45:00 Maya: ok, to recap — Redwood runs benchmarks on your sanitized model + prompts; we'll produce perf report with kernel recommendations, quantization candidate results, and deployment checklist. schedule follow-up week of 2026-04-07.
00:45:30 Samir: agreed. one ask — can you try q4 on a small eval set to surface regressions?
00:45:35 Alex: yes, include q4 and q8 with token-level diffs in the report.

00:47:10 Elena: any gotchas with cuda 12.1 vs 12.0? we have some infra pinned to 12.0 today.
00:47:20 Alex: minimal, but some trt kernels use new APIs; we'll run with both and flag differences. recommend aligning to the runtime we tested if possible.

00:49:00 Maya: action items recap — Alex to run benchmarks, Samir to provide model/prompt set, Priya to draft kernel selection doc, Maya to share security docs. follow-up call after report.

00:50:15 Samir: thanks everyone, excited to see results.
00:50:20 Toby: quick note — our SRE will record system-level metrics during Redwood run and share.
00:51:00 Alex: perfect. we'll coordinate access and upload locations via the AE thread.
00:52:40 Maya: any final questions?
00:52:45 Jordan: none from security side beyond documents.
00:52:50 Elena: all good.
00:53:00 Maya: thanks all, we'll be in touch.

END: recap and next steps agreed.
\REFERENCES/ARTIFACTS MENTIONED: shared nvtx traces link (internal), kernel-timeline.pdf (in chat), Redwood-kernel-flags.md (will be shared), perf-benchmark-template.csv (will be shared).
